messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh Tran, a 52-year-old HVAC technician, traced the beginning of his problems to a service call nine months earlier at a small industrial laundry on the edge of town. He had gone into a poorly ventilated back utility room to inspect a malfunctioning cooling unit. As he worked, there was a sharp chemical smell he could not place at first, then a sudden burning in his nose and throat. Within seconds his eyes were watering, his chest tightened, and he had the frightening sense that the air itself had turned against him. He remembered stumbling toward the door, coughing hard, disoriented and certain that if he did not get out immediately he might collapse alone in that room before anyone found him. Even after emergency evaluation found no lasting organ damage, the experience stayed with him as proof that danger could be present without warning and that reassurance arrived too late to matter.

In the weeks after the exposure, Minh did not feel as though the event had ended. He said that other people, including his wife and the physicians, kept telling him he was safe now, but he found that impossible to believe. What frightened him most was how ordinary the day had seemed before the chemical hit him; if danger had been hidden once in the air around him, he was certain it could be hidden again. His body remained keyed up, his shoulders tight, jaw clenched, breathing shallow, as if he needed to be ready to move at any second. At home he began checking the doors and windows repeatedly at night, going back to the front lock after he had already tested it, then circling to the sliding door and the windows, not because he thought a burglary was especially likely but because he no longer trusted the feeling of safety inside a building. He said the moment of trying to settle down in the evening had become its own kind of alarm; stillness gave him too much room to notice how vulnerable he felt.

That persistent sense that safety could not be trusted began to shape how he lived. Because his body stayed on alert and reassurance did not register, Minh stopped allowing himself to relax. If he sat back on the couch, closed his eyes, or tried to rest on a day off, he quickly became uneasy, feeling that letting his guard down would leave him exposed. He also started avoiding being alone in rooms or buildings. On service calls he would linger near open doorways, ask a coworker to stay close, or find reasons to postpone work in enclosed mechanical spaces if nobody else was around. The idea of being by himself behind a closed door brought him back to the utility room where the air had turned dangerous with no warning. For similar reasons he began avoiding anything he thought might be stressful. He turned down more complicated jobs, tried to keep his route predictable, and delayed calls at facilities that might involve chemical systems or confined work areas. In his mind this caution was not excessive; it was the only way to prevent being caught off guard again.

Over the following months these habits narrowed his world. At work, where HVAC repair had once depended on his ability to enter unfamiliar spaces and stay calm while troubleshooting, he became known for preferring outside units or simple residential jobs. His supervisor noticed that he was taking longer on routine calls because he kept stepping out to “get air” or to recheck exits. At home his wife saw him make a final round of the house and then another, pressing on locks, glancing at windows, listening for anything unusual. She wanted him to sit with her and watch television at night, but relaxing beside her felt dangerous to him, almost irresponsible, and if she went upstairs he often followed rather than remain alone in the living room. He understood that this was straining the household, yet the alternative felt worse. If he stopped scanning, stopped checking, stopped arranging things so that someone else was nearby, he was certain he would miss the next sign of danger.

By the time he sought help, Minh was exhausted by how vigilant he felt and by how small his life had become. He came in after refusing a lucrative solo service job in a commercial building and then arguing with his wife when she told him he could not keep living as though every room might poison him. He said he wanted to believe her when she told him he was home and safe, but he could not make that belief stick. What he feared most was being trapped again in an ordinary place that suddenly became lethal, with no time to react. What he hoped for, cautiously, was to be able to work a full day, sit in his own house at night, and let himself breathe without feeling that doing so was a mistake.
